title: Revivo Clinic Launches Diabetes Remission Programme in Chennai, Screening First
excerpt: The Chennai metabolic-health clinic will assess eligibility and likelihood of remission before enrolment, and says patients who do not qualify will be steered to standard evidence-based diabetes care instead.
body:
• Revivo Clinic in Chennai launched its Type II Diabetes Remission Programme on October 26, ahead of World Diabetes Day on November 14, with enrolment only after a structured clinical evaluation.
  • The physician-led programme combines medical care, personalised nutrition, physical activity and lifestyle support with regular monitoring, and patients who are not eligible are advised on standard evidence-based diabetes management instead.
  • The clinic has published no remission rate for the programme, and its co-founder Dr. Arun Raghavan says remission is scientifically feasible but requires consistent clinical oversight — it is not presented as a cure.
  • For readers in Chennai: the first step is an eligibility assessment at the clinic, not enrolment — bring your recent blood reports and medication list so suitability and likelihood of remission can be judged before you commit.

Revivo Clinic, a Chennai-based centre specialising in obesity, diabetes and metabolic health, has launched a Type II Diabetes Remission Programme, the clinic announced on October 26. The launch, timed ahead of World Diabetes Day on November 14, was formally inaugurated by Dr. Soumiya Anbumani, a Member of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly, and presented by Dr. Arun Raghavan, a diabetologist and metabolic physician who co-founded the clinic.

The programme is built around assessment before treatment. Each person is first put through a structured clinical evaluation that judges eligibility and the likelihood of achieving remission, according to the clinic. Those who are not eligible are advised on evidence-based diabetes management instead.

What the programme actually involves

For those accepted, the programme is physician-led and combines four elements: medical care, personalised nutrition, physical activity and lifestyle interventions, supported by regular monitoring of clinical outcomes. No drug, diet brand or remission percentage is named in the launch material. That restraint matters, because remission claims in diabetes care are easy to overstate.

"Diabetes remission is scientifically feasible, but it requires consistent clinical oversight. Rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all approach, our priority is to assess each individual's suitability for the programme."

— Dr. Arun Raghavan, Diabetologist and Co-Founder, Revivo Clinic

Arvind Ashok, the clinic's fitness and nutrition coach and lifestyle consultant, framed the lifestyle side in local rather than imported terms. Improving lifestyle, he said, does not mean adopting a Western diet; the clinic's pitch is a return to basics — clean eating and healthier everyday choices made accessible and sustainable for people living with diabetes.

A clinic built between the hospital and the gym

Revivo itself is new. The clinic was inaugurated in Chennai in February 2026 by Tamil Nadu Health Minister Ma. Subramanian, with Dr. Raghavan and Aravind Ashok, also a co-founder of fitness venture The Quad, as its founders. Its stated model is to sit between hospitals and gyms: diagnostics, physician-led decision-making and supervised lifestyle execution under one roof. The remission programme is its flagship extension of that model.

Why remission needs careful language

Remission is not the same as a cure, and the distinction is central to how readers should judge any such programme. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes that type 2 diabetes is a serious condition in which the body cannot effectively use insulin, that prediabetes can often be reversed, and that type 2 diabetes can be prevented or delayed with lifestyle changes — language that stops well short of promising that established diabetes will disappear. The CDC also lists the stakes of poor control: heart attack, stroke, blindness and kidney failure.

The need in India is large. The ICMR-INDIAB study found diabetes in 11.4% of Indian adults — about 101 million people — and prediabetes in a further 15.3%. At the launch, Dr. Anbumani called India the diabetes capital of the world and praised the clinic for emphasising early detection, sustained treatment and healthier lifestyle choices, including clean eating. Those figures explain the market for remission programmes; they do not, by themselves, prove that any single programme works. Revivo has published no outcome data for this programme yet, so its results remain a claim to be tested, not a result to be reported.

What this means for readers

For diaspora families arranging care for parents in Chennai, the practical test is the assessment itself. Ask what eligibility criteria were applied, what monitoring is included, and what standard treatment continues alongside the programme. A programme that screens people out, as Revivo says it does, is making a more credible claim than one that enrols everyone.

What to watch

The next useful information from Revivo would be outcomes: how many people were assessed, how many were enrolled, and what share reached and sustained remission, in absolute terms. Until the clinic publishes that, treat any promise of reversing diabetes, from any provider, as a medical claim that needs numbers behind it.
